newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Shelling blocks Afghan Taleban at key pass.
newsitem.headline: Shelling blocks Afghan Taleban at key pass.

text.p: Opposition shelling overnight and on Monday held up a planned advance by Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic militia through the strategic Salang Pass, witnesses said.
They said the Taleban fighters were trying to take positions on mountaintops overlooking the road by forces commanded by renowned guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
Both sides were using artillery and rockets, the witnesses said. There was no immediate information about casualties.
The Taleban fighters were also facing the technical problem of bridging a gap across the road left when retreating opposition fighters blew up a bridge, the witnesses said.

The Taleban convoy on Sunday had reached at the pass, Afghanistan's north-south gateway north of the capital Kabul, seeking to cross into opposition territory after a peace deal with a local pro-Masood commander, Basir Salangi.

"The people of Salang have made an uprising against the forces of evil and corruption, and I call on all the people of Salang to rise against the communists, Salangi told a crowd of Taleban fighters on Sunday.
Salangi had come to an agreement with a council of Taleban commanders in the town of Jabal os-Siraj, at the foot of the Salang Pass.

He called his fighters by a walkie-talkie on Sunday to tell them of the agreement. Thousands of Taleban fighters, loaded on tanks, trucks and four-wheel drive jeeps, cheered Salangi as he was driven up towards the front line.
The fighters anticipated an easy advance through the 11,000-foot (3,350-metre) pass to the northern limits of Salangi's command, the village of Khinjan.
But artillery shells fell close to the waiting Taleban convoy as equipment was brought up to repair the bridge.
The deal to hand over the Salang came a day after forces allied to the Taleban took Mazar-i-Sharif in the north of Afghanistan, the opposition's capital.

Remaining opposition forces are being squeezed by Taleban forces moving south from Mazar-i-Sharif and north from Kabul. Masood, the chief military commander of the government ousted from Kabul by the Taleban last September, is holding out in the Panjsher valley close to the Salang Pass.

Taleban fighters said they believed that Masood's forces were responsible for the shelling of the convoy. If the Salang falls, as the Taleban expect, it will cut the last link between Masood and Hezb-i-Wahadat, a mainly Shi'ite faction still fighting to retain control of central Afghanistan's Bamiyan province.

A Taleban spokesman, quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, said on Monday that the Taleban government had asked the Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat faction to send a delegation to Kabul immediately for peace talks or face a forcible takeover.

The fall of Mazar-i-Sharif, the opposition's main point of supply as well as their political capital, dealt a severe blow to the opposition. They now control less than 10 percent of the country and are confined to mountainous territory in the northeast and centre of Afghanistan.
